text:
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

Devocht v. Hallgren,

2015 BCSC 149

Date: 20150203

Docket:
S62097

Registry: Nanaimo

Between:

Barry
Grant Devocht, Joy Morine Devocht,

Hyung
Min Chung, Jung Ja Lee and

Good
People Estates Ltd.

Plaintiffs

And

Marvin
W. Hallgren, Peter G.V. Faulkner and

Hallgren
& Faulkner Law Corporation

Defendants

Before: The Honourable Mr. Justice Armstrong

Reasons for Judgment

Counsel for the Plaintiffs, Devocht, and

Good People Estates Ltd:

R.J.
Dumonceaux

Counsel for the Defendants:

S.G.
Cordell

Place and Date of Trial:

Nanaimo,
B.C.

October
3, 2014

Place and Date of Judgment:

Nanaimo,
B.C.

February
3, 2015

[
1
]

In this proceeding, the plaintiffs Barry
Devocht, Joy Devocht (the “personal plaintiffs”) and Good People Estates Ltd. (“Good
People”) seek damages for solicitor’s negligence arising from their acquisition
of development property in Jordan River, BC. These reasons concern the defendants’
application to require the three plaintiffs to post security for costs in the
amount of $150,000 before proceeding with this damages action.

[
2
]

The plaintiffs Hyung Min Chung (“Chung”) and
Jung Ja Lee (“Lee”) have assigned their claims to the personal plaintiffs and
have filed discontinuances of their claims in this proceeding.

Background

[
3
]

On June 7, 2006 the plaintiffs Barry Devocht and
Chung agreed to purchase Lot 1 Trailhead Drive (the “land”) from Totangi Forestry
Ltd. with the intention of subdividing the land into strata lots and
constructing residences for resale. Their plan was to separate the lands into
three phases and proceed with development and construction of six strata lots
comprising the first phase of the project.

[
4
]

When the plaintiffs entered into the contract of
purchase and sale of the land (the “contract”), there was an existing statutory
building scheme registered against the title. There was an addendum to the
contract making their agreement "subject to the buyers and seller agreeing
as to the plans and construction of buildings the buyers plan to build by July
31, 2006”. On July 31, 2006 the parties removed this subject clause.

[
5
]

At the same time the vendor and purchasers added
a new subject clause to the contract stipulating that the contract was "subject
to the seller and buyers agreeing to the form and content of the restrictive
covenant that is to be placed on title at completion to replace the building
scheme that is currently on title by August 20, 2006”.

[
6
]

On August 22, 2006 Mr. Faulkner was
retained to act for the personal plaintiffs in the acquisition of the land. On
August 29, 2006 Mr. Faulkner received a copy of the contract and on August
29, 2006 he received confirmation that the restrictive covenant mentioned in
the contract had been removed.

[
7
]

On September 1, 2006 Mr. Faulkner received
the signed addendum.

[
8
]

On July 28, 2006 the parties executed a letter
of understanding in the following terms:

It is the intent of the developer to place a
restrictive covenant at completion, on Lot 1 Trailhead Drive, to replace the
building scheme that will be removed from title at completion. The restrictive
covenant will allow the building of the lodge and cabins approximately as shown
on the revised plan of the lot done by West Coast and Designs LTD, dated July 17,
2006 and will allow the lot to be used for tourist commercial as discussed.

[
9
]

On September 1, 2006 the parties entered into
another addendum to the contract (the addendum) that included the following
terms:

(a)       the seller agreed not to require the buyer to comply with
the terms of the existing statutory building scheme (“SBS”) but rather would
allow the buyer to develop the property in accordance with the provisions of
the modified building scheme attached as Schedule A (the “modified SBS”);

(b)       if the buyer did not develop the property in accordance
with the modified SBS, the seller, at its option, was entitled to require the
buyer to comply with the existing SBS without any claim by the buyer against
the seller for cost charges or expenses; and

(c)        if the buyer did not complete the purchase of the
property as contemplated in the contract of purchase and sale, or transferred
their interest in the contract, then the agreement to permit the buyer to
develop the property in accordance with the modified SBS became null and void
and of no effect.

[
10
]

Good People was incorporated September 1, 2006.
The personal plaintiffs are the sole officers and directors of the company.

[
11
]

The completion of the contract of purchase and
sale was October 20, 2006.

[
12
]

In November 2006 Mr. Hallgren was retained
to incorporate Good People and transfer title of the land to Good People and to
prepare a disclosure statement to allow for the interest in the land to be
sold. Good People was organized and the property transferred to it but no
disclosure statement was prepared. Mr. Devocht was having trouble
obtaining financing and was uncertain about the legal structure he wished to
use for development of the land.

[
13
]

The sale of all of the land to the personal plaintiffs
completed without the registration of the modified SBS as contemplated in the September
1, 2006 amendment. By not registering the modified SBS before sale of the lot
to the buyers (Barry Devocht and Chung), the vendor lost the ability to amend
the SBS without obtaining consent of others who might have been affected by
that instrument. Some of the other persons with an interest in the development
of the property declined to consent to filing the modified SBS, and in the end,
the plaintiffs were required to obtain court approval to modify the SBS.

[
14
]

The plaintiffs obtained tentative financing for
the development project from Canadian Western Bank (“CWB”) for up to $1
million. One condition of the CWB financing required the plaintiffs to have
invested $300,000 in equity. Another condition was that the plaintiffs were obliged
to obtain a minimum of $630,000 in bona fide pre-sales and to deliver copies of
those agreements to the lender. The purpose of the loan was to assist in the
construction of six strata homes.

[
15
]

The plaintiffs’ mortgage commitment contained a
term that the pre-sales were to be “arm’s length" transactions.

[
16
]

In November 2007 Mr. Hallgren was retained
a second time to prepare the disclosure statement. In December 2007 Mr. Hallgren
advised Mr. Devocht about the presence of the SBS on title. Mr. Hallgren
asserts that Mr. Devocht told him he would look into it himself.

[
17
]

On January 21, 2008, the Superintendent of Real Estate
accepted Good People’s disclosure statement for filing. Mr. Devocht head
reviewed and approved the disclosure statement appending a copy of the SBS on
title. In January 2008 Good People retained Mr. Hallgren to assist in
completing the necessary steps to obtain financing from the CWB.

[
18
]

In the summer of 2009 Good People retained Mr. Hallgren
to assist in filing the strata plan with respect to the property. In June 2009 Good
People retained another law firm to assist.

[
19
]

On December 18, 2008 the corporate plaintiff
entered into a contract to sell Lot 3 to Lindsay Salzl (“Salzl”). Salzl was to
deliver a $20,000 deposit. There was a completion date for this purchase of
March 6, 2009, but construction of the unit was not complete by this
date. Salzl extended the completion date of her purchase to April 10, 2009
but her unit was not ready by that time and her mortgage commitment expired
April 16, 2009. In the end she did not purchase a unit and on August 13, 2009
Salzl's deposit was returned to her and the contract ended.

[
20
]

On March 19, 2009 Good People entered into two
separate contracts of purchase and sale for lots, each for $319,900; one sale
was to Chungho Kim (“Kim”) and the other to Younghok Park (“Park”). Kim and
Park were to deliver a $10,000 deposit each.

[
21
]

The completion date for the sales to Kim and
Park was August 15, 2009; both purchasers extended their completion dates to
September 4, 2009. It is apparent from the material that the plaintiffs lent
the deposit monies to Kim and Park. Neither Kim nor Park completed on their
purchases and sometime later Park made an assignment into bankruptcy.

[
22
]

The court order amendment to the SBS was obtained
August 6, 2009. The plaintiffs allege that the delay in obtaining the order
resulted in delays in completing on pre-sales, which resulted in the
prospective buyers refusing to complete their purchases of the developed lot,
which in turn caused a complete collapse of the project and the plaintiffs’
losses.

[
23
]

The plaintiffs claim damages by reason of the defendants’
failure to advise of the consequences of taking title to the land without the
registration of the modified SBS. Their notice of civil claim includes the
following:

32.       As a result of the failure of the
defendants or any of them, to ensure registration of the amended building
scheme on September 1, 2006, the plaintiffs or any of them have been put to
costs and expense, particulars of which include but are not limited to:

(a)        inability
to complete the sales of strata lots as a result of the rejection of the
registration of the strata plan by the Land Title Office, causing the loss of
three purchase and sale transactions, and causing increased interest, principal
and other payments;

(b)        legal
fees and expenses to make application to the Supreme Court to register the
amended building scheme on title to the property;

(c)        inability
of the defendants or any of them to keep payments to subtrades current as a
result of the loss of the sales;

(d)        inability
of the defendants or any of them to keep their obligations to their mortgagee,
Canadian Western Bank current;

(e)        the
costs and expenses of the foreclosure proceeding arising therefrom, as a result
of the loss of the sales;

(f)        because
of the foreclosure proceeding, inability of the plaintiff to obtain financing
to complete three strata units which were only partially completed at the time
of original submission for registration of the strata plan in April, 2009;

(g)        loss
of reputation of the plaintiffs and the strata project, resulting in greater
difficulty selling units, lower prices being offered than the original three
sales, and inability to properly market the project due to inability to
complete unfinished units and incompleted landscaping;

[
24
]

The plaintiffs alleged that the delay between
April 2009 and August 2009 in obtaining court approval of an amended SBS also contributed
to their inability to obtain increased bank financing. The plaintiffs’ lack of
funds in addition to loss of pre-sales led to the eventual collapse of the entire
project. The plaintiffs lost the lands in foreclosure brought by CWB.

[
25
]

The plaintiffs argue that if they had been
properly advised, they would not have entered into contract terms that
contemplated an amendment to the SBS; they contend they would have insisted on
registration of the modified SBS before paying for the land. If the modified SBS
had been in place, the plaintiffs would have met CWB mortgage requirements and
the plaintiffs would have secured pre-sales of two lots for an expected
purchase price of $666,000.

[
26
]

The defendants argue that the collapse of the
overall plan of the plaintiffs to develop the land into their strata properties
with residences failed because they did not have the financial resources to
prosecute the development. Furthermore the Park and Kim agreements were not arm’s
length and the plaintiffs would have been deemed in breach of the mortgage
commitment. The defendants contend that the plaintiffs had attempted to defraud
CWB into advancing a portion of the loan proceeds without having secured bona
fide offers to purchase.

[
27
]

Nevertheless, in April 2009 the plaintiffs were
short of money; they were desperate to find as little as $600 to pay for hydro
installation work. The Salzl transaction had expired and the Kim and Park
agreements were extended to September 4, 2009, well after the court order was
obtained on August 15, 2009.

[
28
]

This proceeding was commenced with a notice of
civil claim filed January 28, 2011. Between February and July 2011 the parties
exchanged requests for documents and engaged in settlement discussions. Those
discussions ended July 14, 2011 and in January 2013 the plaintiffs retained new
counsel who communicated a new settlement proposal. In September 2013 the
plaintiffs retained Mr. Dumonceaux to represent them in this proceeding.
In December 2013, he advised defence counsel that he did not act for Chung or Lee.

[
29
]

Motivated by concerns about the plaintiffs’
impecuniosity and the costs they will incur in this litigation, on June 16, 2014
the defendants filed this application seeking an order that the personal
plaintiffs and Good People be required to pay security for costs in an amount
of $150,000.

[
30
]

There is no issue on this application that the
defendants have not applied for a security costs order in a timely way.

The Plaintiffs’ Resources

[
31
]

The defendants’ investigation of Good People’s
financial circumstances reveals that it owns no real property in British
Columbia. The defendants performed searches of the registry kept under the
Personal
Property Security Act
, RSBC 1996, c. 359; this revealed evidence of registrations
encumbering any other assets owned by the company but no other assets were
found in the name of the company.

[
32
]

The title to the land was foreclosed and the
plaintiffs have no continuing interest in the development.

[
33
]

The defendants’ investigation discloses that the
personal plaintiffs own a home in Victoria with an apparent value of $405,500,
against which there are mortgages registered with a principal amount of
$367,500 securing current and running accounts. The defendants rely on a 2014
BC Assessment Authority web query for this information.

[
34
]

There is an issue concerning the use of
assessment information as evidence of value. In
Dosanjh v. Liang
,
2015
BCCA 18
[
Dosanjh
] Groberman J.A. recently considered this question:

[62]      It seems to me that different
considerations arise in non-family cases, where one party or the other will
generally bear the onus of producing evidence of property value.

[63]      It is not necessary, in this case,
to make any pronouncement as to the scope for admission of property assessments
as evidence of property value in family law cases, and I will refrain from
doing so. In my view, however, there is, absent agreement, no scope for using
assessments in place of expert opinion evidence in cases such as the present
one.

[
35
]

Dosanjh
involved
a situation where a real estate transaction failed to complete due to the
vendor’s repudiation of the contract. The purchaser accepted the repudiation
and sought damages. BC Assessments was used to establish damages. In my view,
in light of this authority, if the value of assets available to answer for
costs judgments is in issue, the evidence must be in the form of admissible
opinion evidence.

[
36
]

Mr. Devocht was recently employed in
Alberta in carpentry but in his bankruptcy filing indicates he has no income.
He has been unemployed since August 2014. Mrs. Devocht is employed as a
teacher and earns $4,091 per month. The parties are supporting one adult child.

[
37
]

The personal plaintiffs have made consumer proposals
in bankruptcy which have not been accepted or rejected by their creditors.
Apparently a further meeting was contemplated.

[
38
]

Mrs. Devocht has claimed her RRSP savings
as exempt under the
Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act
, R.S.C. 1985, c. B-3
[
BIA
]. Both individuals have claimed as exempt some of their motor
vehicles, Mr. Devocht’s tools, and their interest in the family home.

[
39
]

The personal plaintiffs propose to pay $25,046
for the benefit of their unsecured creditors, whose claims total $136,165. This
proposal includes an immediate payment of $20,000 followed by 58 monthly
instalments of $87 per month. They propose to use $663 per month from their
income to pay secured creditors totalling $399,175.

[
40
]

I note that if the proposal is rejected or the
personal plaintiffs breach any commitment in their proposals, then the personal
plaintiffs will become bankrupt. The
BIA
provides:

Result of refusal of proposal

57.       Where
the creditors refuse a proposal in respect of an insolvent person,

(
a
)        the
insolvent person is deemed to have thereupon made an assignment;

(
b
)        the
trustee shall, without delay, file with the official receiver, in the
prescribed form, a report of the deemed assignment;

(
b.1
)     the
official receiver shall issue a certificate of assignment, in the prescribed
form, which has the same effect for the purposes of this
Act
as an assignment
filed under
section 49
; and

The Defendants’ Position

[
41
]

The defendants estimate their taxable costs and
disbursements through to the conclusion of a trial in this proceeding as
$152,819. The plaintiffs do not take any issue with this estimate. Document
production is incomplete and the defendants do not have accounting evidence, a
list of all witnesses, or the steps necessary to obtain evidence. The defendants
argue that “in all of the circumstances” it would be just to order security for
costs at $150,000 as against the corporate plaintiff and personal plaintiffs.

[
42
]

The defendants argue that the plaintiffs’ claims
are weak and conversely their defence is strong.

[
43
]

They contend:

(a)       Mr. Devocht does not deny he was advised, at the time
of purchase, that the SBS remained on title or that he was told that the SBS
would have to be removed from title before registration of a strata plan;

(b)       there was no evidence that pre-sales were lost because of
the three month delay in registering a strata plan; they collapsed for other
reasons. Even if they were at arm’s length, the Kim and Park pre-sale contracts
were ratified and extended to September 4, 2009 so they were contractually
bound to complete after the three month delay but were released from their
contracts by the plaintiffs;

(c)        the Salzl pre-sale did not complete because construction
was slow and her mortgage commitment had expired; and

(d)       the evidence does not suggest that the three month delay
in registering a strata plan affected any CWB funding.

[
44
]

The defendants argue that the possibility that the
plaintiffs will be deterred from pursuing a claim is not, without more detailed
evidence, sufficient reason for not ordering security for costs. They contend
that a plaintiff must first demonstrate that they have no way of raising funds
to continue litigation if an award of costs is made against them; in this case
they say the plaintiffs have failed.

[
45
]

The defendants point to a carefully worded
affidavit by Mrs. Devocht in which she said:

… I confirm that I do not have access to any
other line of credit or credit cards, from which I could draw funds to pay
money into court as security for costs.

[
46
]

Mr. Devocht deposed in his affidavit:

The consumer proposal lists accurately all
the assets I own and I confirm that I do not have access to any other line of
credit or credit cards, from which I could draw funds to pay money into court
as security for costs.

[
47
]

Neither of the personal plaintiffs has addressed
the possibility of obtaining other financial assistance from family or friends
or other bank loans. They seem to have found money from an outside source to
help in making their proposal payments. Earlier in 2014 the parties managed to
obtain an increase in their mortgage debt, part of which is also to be used to
fund their bankruptcy proposal.

[
48
]

Neither plaintiff deposed that an order for
security for costs would stifle the litigation. Neither plaintiff described any
efforts they have made to obtain financial assistance. Their comment on this
point was limited to their assertions that they are unable to access further credit
card debt or lines of credit.

[
49
]

The defendants argue that if the court refuses
to order security posted by the personal plaintiffs, this should not influence
the decision to order the corporate plaintiff to post security. The defendants
point out that corporate plaintiffs are treated more harshly when it comes to
security for costs orders, the policy reason being that the individuals behind
a corporation face less risk in pursing litigation because they are protected
by the corporate veil:
Krupp v. Swansea Bay Golf Course Ltd.
(1997)
,
1997 CanLII 4037 (BC CA)
, 29
B.C.L.R. (3d) 252 (C.A.)

[
Kropp
]. The defendants argue that the
less stringent test should continue to apply to the corporate plaintiff in this
case, notwithstanding the suggestion in
Hawksview Enterprises Ltd. v.
British Columbia Hydro and Power Authority,
2014 BCSC 226
[
Hawksview
]
that the more stringent test generally applied to individuals may be applied to
corporate plaintiffs when an individual and corporate plaintiff are both
alleging the same cause of action and damages. The defendants argue that
Hawksview

is distinguishable or wrongly decided and is inconsistent with the decision
in
Kropp
.

[
50
]

The defendants argue that the less stringent
test also applies to Good People because the pleadings in this case do not
discriminate between interests of each of the corporate and personal
plaintiffs’ interests, nor is it clear whether the personal plaintiffs suffered
any damage. The CWB financing was offered to Good People subject to the
personal plaintiffs providing a personal guarantee.

The Plaintiffs Position

[
51
]

The plaintiffs contend that the court’s
discretion to order security for costs against individuals is limited to
special circumstances, sometimes described as egregious circumstances.

[
52
]

They argue that the less demanding test
applicable to security for costs applications concerning corporation’s proceeds
from the assumption that the individuals behind the corporation face little
risk in pursuing the litigation. The underlying policy is to protect the
community against the abuse created when an artificial person is manipulated by
a natural person. In this case they suggest that because the personal plaintiffs
will be jointly liable with the corporate plaintiff, the policy directed
against limited liability corporations avoiding costs is not engaged.

[
53
]

The plaintiffs rely on
Hawksview
for this
submission,

where the court indicated that applications for security for
costs addressed to personal and corporate plaintiffs alleging the same cause of
action and damages should not notionally be subdivided between individuals and
corporations. The more stringent principles of the test generally applied to
individuals should apply to each plaintiff in this case, notwithstanding the
general rule that corporations will be treated less stringently.

[
54
]

The plaintiffs point out that the defendants
recognize that to obtain an order for security against a corporation might
stifle the action because the plaintiffs have no assets or means of raising
money for security.

[
55
]

The plaintiffs contend that their current
financial difficulties have been contributed to by the negligence of the defendants;
this factor should weigh heavily against an order for security for costs.

[
56
]

The plaintiffs submit that they have a
compelling case against the solicitors. Mr. Devocht denied any
sophistication in the land development business. He denies being advised by his
solicitor that the land was not ready for development because the statutory
building scheme could not be modified without court order. That order was not
obtained until August 6, 2009 at which point all of the pre-sales previously
negotiated by the plaintiffs had collapsed.

[
57
]

The plaintiffs contend that any order for
security will result in a dismissal of the claim. They are currently under a
bankruptcy proposal and are attempting to achieve an agreement to pay creditors
$25,000 in satisfaction of more than $500,000 consumer debt.

[
58
]

In the absence of any certainty that the
statutory building scheme would be approved, the viability of the development
was at risk. They contend that the financial collapse of the project and their inability
to fund this litigation is a direct consequence of the failure of the real
estate development contributed to by the negligence of the defendants. Thus, it
would be inappropriate to require them to post security.

The Law

[
59
]

There are three issues to be decided on this application.
I will consider:

(a)       what test for granting security for costs should apply to
the corporate plaintiff;

(b)       whether an order for security for costs should be made
against the personal plaintiffs; and

(c)        whether an order for security for costs should be made
against the corporate plaintiff.

[
60
]

The power to order a corporate plaintiff to post
security for costs is a function of the court’s inherent jurisdiction and the
statutory provisions of the
Business Corporations Act
, S.B.C. 2002,
c. 57 [
Act
].
Section 236
of the
Act
provides:

236.     If a corporation is the plaintiff
in a legal proceeding brought before the court, and if it appears that the
corporation will be unable to pay the costs of the defendant if the defendant
is successful in the defence, the court may require security to be given by the
corporation for those costs, and may stay all legal proceedings until the
security is given.

[
61
]

The principles underlying security for costs
applications were settled in
Kropp
. The court described the principles
from
Keary Development v. Tarmac Construction
,
[1995] 3 All E.R. 534
as
a useful summary of the applicable guide to considerations under the
Act
.
They include:

1.         The court has a complete discretion whether to order
security, and will act in light of all the relevant circumstances;

2.         The possibility or probability that the plaintiff company
will be deterred from pursuing its claim is not, without more sufficient
evidence, reason for not ordering security;

3.         The court must attempt to balance injustices arising from
use of security as an instrument of oppression to stifle a legitimate claim on
the one hand, and use of impecuniosity as a means of putting unfair pressure on
a defendant on the other;

4.         The court may have regard to the merits of the action, but
should avoid going into detail on the merits unless success or failure appears
obvious;

5.         The court can order any amount of security up to the full
amount claimed, as long as the amount is more than nominal;

6.         Before the court refuses to order security on the ground
that it would unfairly stifle a valid claim, the court must be satisfied that,
in all the circumstances, it is probable that the claim would be stifled; and

7.         The lateness of the application for security is a
circumstance which can properly be taken into account.

[
62
]

At the outset, the applicant must prove a
prima
facie
case that the plaintiff company is unable to pay the applicant’s
costs if the claim fails. If the applicant meets this evidentiary burden, then
the plaintiff company may be relieved of the burden of security if it can show
it has sufficient eligible assets to satisfy an award for costs or if there is
no arguable defence to the claim:
Integrated Contractors Ltd. v. Leduc
Development Ltd
.,
2009 BCSC 965
;
Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v.
Canadian Jewish Congress
(1999),
1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
, 36 CPC (4th) 266 (B.C.S.C.).

[
63
]

Once the applicant has proved a
prima facie

case that the plaintiff does not have exigible assets, the burden to prove the
existence of such assets shifts to the plaintiff. Absent such evidence the
general rule is to order security for costs unless there is no arguable defence:

Fat Mel’s Restaurant Ltd. v. Canadian Northern Shield Insurance Co
. (1993),

1993 CanLII 1669 (BC CA)
, 76 B.C.L.R. (2d) 231 (C.A.) [
Fat Mel’s
] at para.
16
.

[
64
]

There is no rule of court governing when an
order should be made for security for costs against an individual; it is
entirely within the court’s discretion and inherent jurisdiction:
Han v.
Cho,
2008 BCSC 1229
[
Han
].

[
65
]

Natural persons will not ordinarily be required
to post security for costs unless some egregious or extraordinary circumstances
merit such an order. This aspect of the application requires a balancing of the
interests of justice between the parties in an effort to ensure that the
substance of the dispute is properly litigated and the personal plaintiffs are
not deprived of access to the court due to impecuniosity:
Han
.

[
66
]

Special circumstances that may justify cost
security orders against personal plaintiffs include the fact that the plaintiff
has failed to pay other cost orders. The categories of behaviours that might
warrant a security for costs order against individuals is not closed, but it is
clear that impecuniosity is not a basis for ordering security from an individual:

Deepak Suri Ltd. v Urban Choice Market Ltd.
,
2013 BCSC 2460
.

[
67
]

The court may consider the merits of the
plaintiff’s claim but should avoid a detailed analysis of those merits unless
failure appears obvious. The onus of proving the absence of an arguable defence
is on the plaintiff:
Fat Mel’s
at para. 236.

[
68
]

The cause of action in and of itself is not an
asset that can be relied upon by the plaintiff to resist an award of security
for costs:
Malahat Marble Products Ltd. v. Anderson
(1955),
1955 CanLII 566 (BC CA)
, 14 W.W.R.
697 (B.C.C.A.) at p. 698.

[
69
]

The court will not order security if such an
order would unfairly stifle a valid claim:
Kropp
at para.
17
. Where
financial hardship is due to the actions of the applicant in the case, an order
may be refused.

[
70
]

In this case, the defendants have met their
burden of demonstrating that Good People has no exigible assets and will not be
able to pay any order for costs from assets currently owned if the action fails.

The Test to Apply to the Corporate Plaintiff

[
71
]

In this case, I am not satisfied that the
circumstances warrant a departure from the principle outlined in
Kropp

that different considerations apply to corporations resisting security for
costs applications. The court said:

[24]      So I am respectfully of the view
that the learned chambers judge erred in finding that the corporate plaintiff
would be prevented from pursuing its claim if security were to be ordered. And
it would, in my view, be contrary to the principles enunciated above to refuse
security on the grounds that the corporate plaintiff would "have
difficulty" in pursuing the action if security for costs were to be
ordered.
It seems likely, as the defendants contend, that the learned
chambers judge failed adequately to distinguish between the position of Mr. Kropp
as a natural person, and the corporate plaintiff as an artificial legal entity.
I think this is entirely understandable, given the failure to distinguish in
the statement of claim between the claims of the two plaintiffs.

[Emphasis added.]

[
72
]

In my view the situation of the corporate
plaintiff is distinguishable from the circumstances described in
Hawksview
.
In
that case, the corporate plaintiff owned a home in which the personal
plaintiffs resided; the home was allegedly damaged by the defendants and the
corporate plaintiff and personal plaintiffs jointly advanced an identical claim
against them. The court applied the more stringent test generally applicable to
individuals and declined to order security for costs against the corporation.

[
73
]

I am cognizant of the approach taken by Holmes
J. in
Hawksview
where she said:

[15]      True, Mr. Cruickshank as one
of Hawksview’s officers and co-owners, enjoys the protection of Hawksview’s
corporate veil in relation to Hawksview’s own liability. However, along with Ms. Hicks,
Mr. Cruickshank pursues the action also in a personal capacity
. The
fact that Hawksview is also a plaintiff in the action does not reduce Mr. Cruickshank’s
and Ms. Hicks’s personal exposure to risk in the litigation as individual
plaintiffs.

…

[17]      Similar reasoning leads me to
conclude that the defendants applications in this case should each be
determined as a whole, according to the test generally applied in relation to
individual plaintiffs. The applications should not be notionally subdivided and
determined, in relation to Hawksview, according to the less demanding test
applied in respect of corporate plaintiffs.

[18]      As I have indicated, the evidence
discloses no special circumstances to support the orders sought. On its face,
the plaintiffs have a reasonable claim against all of the defendants. In my
view, this is not the appropriate context in which to determine the merit of
the claim against the Dickson defendants in the detail necessary for a
determination of whether, as those defendants submit, the claim is bound to
fail; the acknowledgement by BC Hydro’s Gary Nyrose, in his examination for
discovery, that BC Hydro takes full responsibility for identifying and
replacing hazardous trees and vegetation, is not necessarily determinative of
the Dickson defendants’ liability.
There is no evidence that the individual
plaintiffs are impecunious -- indeed, Mr. Cruickshank deposes that he owns
an unencumbered property in Mexico with a value he estimates at approximately
$500,000. Mr. Cruickshank deposes that he has family still living in
British Columbia, including his mother, three children, and two grandchildren,
and travels “home” to British Columbia on a regular basis. I find no basis on
which to conclude that the plaintiffs have failed to deal appropriately with
their financial obligations in the past, or have misconducted themselves in any
way.
Their claim relates to an event which took place when they lived in
B.C., and, on the evidence, it was that event which drove the individual
plaintiffs to move to their recreational property outside the country.

[
74
]

I note the recent case of
603262 B.C. Ltd. v.
Eiyom Properties Ltd.,
2014 BCSC 2389
in which the court distinguished
Hawksview

on the basis that on the facts of that case, it was clear that the
corporate plaintiff’s claim against the defendant was distinct from the
individual plaintiffs’ claim, and as such the individual plaintiffs faced no
personal financial risk from the corporation’s involvement in the litigation.
In addition there had been no application for costs sought against the
individual plaintiffs.

[
75
]

In the case at bar, while the personal
plaintiffs and Good People advance the same cause of action, there is not
enough evidence in the pleadings to determine if the claims of the personal
plaintiffs and of Good People are the same in the manner contemplated by
Hawksview

sufficient to merit the application of the more stringent test to both the
personal plaintiffs and Good People.

[
76
]

The land had been transferred into the names of
the personal plaintiffs without registering the amended SBS contemplated in the
contract. When the land was transferred from the personal plaintiffs to Good
People in November 2006, there was no amended SBS in place. Good People alleges
that its losses more than two years later occurred because it could not
complete sales of its lots with changes to the SBS that were on title from the
date it acquired the land. It is unclear which losses are alleged by the
personal plaintiffs.

[
77
]

Either way, the personal plaintiffs are
insolvent and at risk of becoming bankrupt soon. They have availed themselves
of the
BIA

to shield some of their assets from creditors. Any order of
costs arising from these proceedings would likely force them into bankruptcy;
on bankruptcy, any costs payable by the personal plaintiffs will be
extinguished. They will, in effect, be gambling on the success of their claims without
any risk resulting from a dismissal of their claim. Meanwhile, if the
plaintiffs become bankrupt, Good People will not be affected by their changed
status and will still enjoy the protection of a limited liability company.

[
78
]

If Good People’s claim fails, the resulting
order for costs against Good People will not be payable by the personal
plaintiffs because they will be shielded by both the corporate veil and the
inevitable bankruptcy proceedings; as well if the personal plaintiffs’ claims
against the defendants are sufficiently different from Good People’s claims
such that they will not be jointly liable, the personal plaintiffs will face no
personal financial risk from Good People’s involvement with the litigation. The
defendants will be left without any recourse.

[
79
]

This speaks to the precise policy reason
articulated in
Kropp
why corporate plaintiffs are treated more harshly
in security for costs applications, namely to protect the community against
litigious abuses by artificial persons manipulated by natural persons. As Finch
J.A. highlights in
Kropp
,
quoting the English decision of
Pearson
at
535, “one should be slow to whittle away this protection”.

[
80
]

In my view, the principle outlined in
Kropp

was not diminished by the finding in
Hawksview
. The facts in this case
are distinguishable from those in
Hawksview
and the principle
articulated by Holmes J. has no application to the circumstances before me. The
appropriate test to apply to Good People is the one for corporate litigants.

The Personal Plaintiffs

[
81
]

The personal plaintiffs are insolvent and, in
view of their consumer proposals, have no practical hope of paying a costs
order if their claim is unsuccessful. I think it is more likely that, if the plaintiffs
are unsuccessful, they will become bankrupt soon after as it is unlikely they
will be able to continue to meet their proposal obligations and answer to an order
for costs of $150,000.

[
82
]

The minimal prospects of the defendants
recovering costs at the end of this lawsuit are a punishing disadvantage faced
by the defendants. There is a tension between an impecunious plaintiff and a
legal adversary who is obliged to defend claims with only modest chances of
success. Subject to the outcome in the plaintiff’s proposal, costs that will
accrue between now and trial will be lost to the defendant if the plaintiffs
become bankrupt.

[
83
]

The defendants correctly point out that the
plaintiffs did not disclose the financial circumstances of two closely held
corporations in which they own shares. The plaintiffs did not disclose the
identity of a third party giving them funds to deal with their consumer
proposal. Notwithstanding these shortcomings in their financial disclosure, I
am not convinced that they should be required to post security. In my view,
Beasse
v. Holness
,
2006 BCSC 1265
dealt with circumstances in which the Chambers
Judge found the personal plaintiffs to have been less than truthful in their
affidavit evidence. This is not the case with the personal plaintiffs in this
action.

[
84
]

I do not accept that this tenuous evidence
concerning the personal plaintiffs’ circumstances to be untruthful or
deliberately misleading. Although they have not addressed some of the usual
questions concerning other resources, I am satisfied that this is not an
extraordinary or egregious case which would warrant ordering the personal
defendants to post security for costs. Insolvency alone has never been a basis
for requiring security for costs from personal plaintiffs.

[
85
]

In the final analysis, the principle of keeping
the court accessible to the poorest litigant overrides the risk to more
financially robust parties forced to defend claims where costs of a successful
defence will not likely be paid.

The Corporate Plaintiff

[
86
]

In this case, it is my view that the corporation
must post security for costs.

[
87
]

The court has inherent jurisdiction on
applications to force a corporate plaintiff to post security for costs. Good
People has been shown to own no exigible assets and the defendants have made
out their
prima facie
case that if the corporate defendant is
unsuccessful, they will not likely recover their costs.

[
88
]

There was no promise or undertaking by the
personal plaintiffs to pay a costs order against Good People nor is there any
evidence that the personal plaintiffs’ resources that are exempted from the consumer
bankruptcy proposal will not be available to answer for the defendants’ costs.

[
89
]

The plaintiffs have not said or established that
an order for security for costs will stifle the corporation’s claims in this
litigation. The evidence tendered on this point is equivocal at best and
insufficient on its face. Their evidence demonstrates that they cannot access
any other lines of credit or credit card debt to pay for security for costs.
They have not addressed the question of any other sources of money that might
be available. They were able to secure $10,000 from a third party to facilitate
their consumer proposal. They expect to pay $5,046 over 58 months to satisfy
their unsecured obligations. At this point, it is unknown whether the consumer
proposal is or will be accepted by the creditors.

[
90
]

In view of the personal plaintiffs’
circumstances and the fact that the plaintiffs did not disclose what efforts
they had made to secure financial help to assist them, none of the plaintiffs
have met the burden of showing that the claim will be stifled if they are
required to post security.

[
91
]

I also find that the defendants have an arguable
defence to the claim. On the facts asserted by the defendant, there is
compelling evidence that the plaintiffs did not suffer any loss in reliance on
the advice of the defendants; did not lose the lands due to the delay in
obtaining the August 2009 court order; and may have lost the prospect of
additional financing as a result of misleading CWB.

[
92
]

Further, the pleadings do not assist in
informing the court about the distinctions between Good People’s claims and the
personal plaintiffs’ claims. This issue was specifically mentioned by Finch J.A.
in
Kropp
when addressing an application against a corporate plaintiff
and a personal plaintiff.

[
93
]

The plaintiffs contend that their impecuniosity
is a direct result of the defendant’s negligence in advising them between 2006
and 2009. Their claim identifies the delay in obtaining the registration of the
strata plan from April 2009 to August 2009 as the cause of the loss.

[
94
]

The plaintiffs did not explain why the Kim and
Park transactions did not complete in September 2009. There was no evidence to
explain the results of their efforts to satisfy CWB and finish their project.

Was the Plaintiffs Impecuniosity Caused by the Defendants

[
95
]

The plaintiffs contend that their current
financial circumstances and inability to pay costs were caused by the defendants’
negligence and, as such, an order for security for costs should not be made.

[
96
]

It is clear that the plaintiffs were in
difficult financial straits in March and April 2009. Those shortcomings appear
to have contributed to the loss of Ms. Salzl’s purchase. The plaintiffs’
evidence did not persuade me that their impecuniosity was caused by the defendants’
negligence and not unrelated circumstances affecting their financial affairs. I
infer that the measure and extent of consumer debt disclosed in their proposal
is an indication that other factors adversely impacted their current financial
state contributing to their impecuniosity.

[
97
]

In
Tim Keith Contracting Ltd. v. Richform
Construction Supply Company Limited
,
2010 BCSC 1861
, Schultes J. dealt with
a security for costs application involving a plaintiff with a substantial
number of claims and actions. The court’s comments are apposite:

[45]      As I said in a previous context in
this judgment, the much stronger inference from the number of actions against
the plaintiff and the amounts claimed in them is that the plaintiff has been
defaulting on its financial commitments to a variety of creditors for reasons
that extend beyond its dispute with this defendant.

Conclusion

[
98
]

I order that Good People post security for costs
if it wishes to advance the claims against the defendants.

[
99
]

The amount of security is a matter of discretion
for the Court. In my view, after considering all the evidence and the case
authorities before me, Good People must post security in the amount of $100,000.
The security must be posted within 60 days failing which the defendants will be
entitled to apply for judgment dismissing Good People’s claims.

The Honourable Mr. Justice Armstrong
